cad043ca-7b09-4001-af12-7d68b0d0208b.title: Toyota forklifts serves PSAs new gate
bodies: United Motor Works latest coup is a single tender award for the supply. of 102 units 3 ton diesel driven forklift trucks and ten units 2’ ton battery forklifts to PSA. These forklifts are now operating
at PSA’s new gateway at Pasir Panjang, Singapore. Quite apart from this deal Toyota forklift trucks are currently the largest selling range of material handling equipment in Singapore and Malaysia.

Their range of forklifts available covers 1000 kg to 25000 kg diesel driven forklift trucks, petrol and LP. gas trucks from 700 kg to 6000 kg and battery powered from 500 kg to 4000 kg. The main models are available almost immediately. Forklift trucks have made material handling fast, efficient and indeed safe. With international trade growing and material handling becomingmore than just efficient and neat stacking, forklifts have undergone many innovations in adaptability.

The Toyota forklifts come with many attachments suitable for various diversified industries. For very high lifts a 3-stage mast can be fitted to reach a height of 6500 mm (256”). To load and unload in low holds of ships and containers a 2stage full free lift mast can be attached together with a side-shifter. Their forklifts can also be attached with clamps for work with bales of cotton or pulp, drums and a full 360 rotating clamp for paper rolls. Further versatility of these workhorses is obtained by attaching a ram for coiled goods, a crane arm for lifting objects with slings, hinged forks which can be coupled with bucket, load stabilizers for high stack and fragile cargo. Toyota forklifts come with UMW after sales service guarantee. UMW maintain a large fleet of mobile inspection and service vehicles manned by highly skilled trouble-shooter mechanics. This unit minimises lay down time and regularly inspects Toyota forklifts at worksites to diagnose potential problems free of charge, advise on necessary replacement parts and service the trucks if required. They are on call as well. One UMW spokesman added, “Our motto is — service with expertise.” A mouthful? No, a varifiable fact.

8bdeda19-db38-4a93-9b64-4d5e56b09f62.title: CONTAINERISED PLEASURE BOATS
bodies: Newly-built pleasure boats are becoming a common sight on the decks of containerships these days, as the box carriers are proving a safer and faster mode of transport for high-value cargoes. With the systematic loading and unloading and placement of containers on board, uncontainerisable deck cargoes are not so prone to hard knocks that are common in conventional shipping. American Marine, builder of the Grand Banks range of luxury crafts, over the weekend exported a 32 foot model to a client in Europe. The boat was fixed with a cradle and loaded on board the ScanDutch containership Nedlloyd Delft for a slightly over 20-day trip to Denmark. American Marine, which exports about 10 per cent of its boats to Europe, uses containership transport to ensure the high quality finishing of its crafts remains intact when delivered to customers.

7e37015e-53f0-4f44-a472-437aac0f7f7b.title: New Port Facility Nears Completion
bodies: At the East Lagoon on the northern side of the PSA container terminal , two new container berths are now under construction. These berths will cater increased container traffic expected in the next few years. The first berth will provide a special shore based ramp designed to service the three new vessels of the ANRO Consortium which comprises the Australian National Line, Neptune Orient Lines of Singapore, Australia Straits Container Line and Nedllyod Lines. Completion of the berth is expected by the end of September 1977.

The two berths totalling about S$66 million will be 640 metres in length with two main access bridges linking them to a 19.5 hectare marshalling yard and 10.5 heotares of back up land. The schedule was 18 months for completion of the first berth and 26 months for the complete project. To date the schedule has been maintained. Although the extra capacity provided by the 2 berths will help equip the terminal to cater for the estimated growth in container traffic between now and 1980, the project has been designed to be as flexible as possible. Four 35 tonne portainer cranes purchased at a cost of about $$2.56 million each, plus several transtainer cranes will service the berths. This equipment combined with the modern gear and design of the vessels will help cater for the growth in cargo traffic by improving turn-around times and collection and delivery of cargo. The two new berths will be equipped and fully operational by 1979 just about the same time the existing facilities will have reached their optimum capacity. The construction of the two new berths coincides with the commencement of work on a $$50 million inland container depot at Bukit Timah, about 25 kilometres from the terminal. Its function will be a container storage area and a break bulk consolidation depot.

Their offices are perched symbo lically high in the Chinese Chamber ot! Commerce. Apart from their oilfield material handling they also haul heavy and allied equipment. The company maintains a fleet of nearly thirty heavy loaders with a range of three to sixty-five tons individually. Their clients have the added advantage of total service in the form of shipping and air freight documentation both for inward and outward destinations. Shipping and airfreight offices are located within the same roof, thus saving time and effort. Boswell also own boats and barges and have their own crew and boarding officers. This makes it easier for them to carry out their work efficiently and in the shortest time possible. The company’s efficiency rating is pretty high due mainly to the fact that it has its own workshops for maintenance. As a result of this facility special loads are always escorted by another vehicle carrying qualified mechanics, spares and ancilliary neces: sities in the event of a breakdown. This mini-

mises breakdown time and the expensive and time consuming process of transferring loads from the breakdown vehicle to another. Add to this the fact that their staff is highly experienced and have been with the company for some years. Their loyalty is total and their personal interest in the safe, fast and economical delivery of loads. In a brief conversation with the Singapore Shipping and Air Gazette, Mr Jeorji Boswell, a director of the company said, “We are a service organisation and as such we must be very thorough in our systems. Millions of dollars worth of goods pass through our hands, because of trust. Therefore we cannot afford mistakes.” Boswell International operates on more than 95% local staff, whom they look after well. Only the top echelon executives are | expatriates. : What is amazing is that the company, | while being very modern in its operations, is able to remain highly competitive in charges _ and in some instances even lower than the | test of the transport companies. This is perhaps possible because of their being almost self sufficient. We say almost because they do not own an oilfield.

3ab970fd-776d-4105-b710-bda0f8385bf3.title: RADIOISOTOPE ON STREAM ANALYSIS OF MINERALS
bodies: A RELIABLE and economic method of on-stream analysis for increasing the efficiency of mineral processing is offered by the Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (AMDEL). AMDEL is a contract research organisation providing technical development and consulting services to industry and government in the fields of mineral and material sciences. ‘The on-stream analytical system, using radioisotope immersion probes, has application to heavy metal processing for elements above titanium in the Periodic Table, in larger-scale modern plant. It provides a method of-continuous automatic readout of metal values in process slurry streams, enabling the most efficient operation of mineral processing plant. The highly significant break-through in this new method of analysis has been the Australian development of a range of immersible probes, each housing a detector head assembly, a scintillation counter and a radioisotope source . The probes are designed to measure mineral content and slurry density, with an accuracy practical to the application, using both X-ray fluorescence and X-ray gammaray absorption techniques, while actually immersed in the Process streams. _ The probes aré inexpensive, of rugged construction and easy to install and to replace. Components of the on-stream analytical system are designed and manufactured by AMDEL will research and development support from the Australian Atomic Energy Commission. The Australian Mineral Industry Research Association and the Zinc Corporation. Under the terms of a worldwide agreement, AMDEL carries out the necessary feasibility studies, and designs, manufactures and installs the equipment. The system is sufficiently flexible to allow step-bystep growth from a basic analysis arrangement to one involving fully computerised plant control with feedback from a number of points in the process. Because of this flexibility, the cost of the installation can be effectively controlled to suit the size of the plant. The cost of the equipment, although a half to a third that of competitors, is likely to be about $A113,000 fora typical 3-stream installation. The IOSA immersion probe system has now a proved history of operation for more than five years in Australia and abroad, for copper, lead, zinc, nickel and tin. AMDEL’s services and facilities include: Analytical chemistry, mineralogy, petrology, geochemistry, geochronology, materials technology, ‘operations research, computer services, geostatistics, mine planning, mineral engineering, chemical metallugry, instrumentation, water treatment, process development, feasibility studies, pat design and commissioning. fccfee21-57e3-43b4-a11b-f601f632de1f.title: ASEA’S NEW METHOD TO CONTAIN NUCLEAR WASTE
bodies: ASEA, the Swedish worldwide manufacturer of electrical and mechanical equipment, is working on the development of a process using hot isostatic pressing for the safe containment and storage of nuclear waste. This development work which is being carried out at the Company’s High-Pressure Laboratory at Robertsfors, in the north of Sweden, promises to contain all dangers in the disposal of nuclear waste. Under high pressure the waste is compacted together to form a dense and solid body which is harder than any kind of rock including granite! this process which is called hot isostatic pressing, is already been used in some of ASEA’s products, for instance, the Quintus Presses marketed throughout the world including Singapore. This new method will not only interest countries who are now grappling with the nuclear waste problem, but also others like the Republic who are seriously considering nuclear energy as an alternative power to oil. ASEA has been working in the field of highpressure research since the 1940s and has developed a number of processes and products which have led to important breakthroughts in materials technology.

9b108d02-6535-4aa1-94cc-ad21e292cdc6.title: BARBER BLUE SEA — NEW VESSELS
bodies: Barber Blue Sea (BBS) is planning to introduce new vessels on their Far East - USA — Far East routes in 1977. In an announcement Kaare B Isaksen, Senior Vice President of BBS, said: “M S ‘TSU’ now enroute from Japan to Panama on her maiden voyage is due Miami on June 14. This is the first of ten new Combo Class vessels being built for BBS to replace some of our present fleet and we expect all ten vessels to be in operation by the end of 1977. ~ The ten new Combo Class vessels will supplement similar type of vessels already operating successfully in the BBS Service to Panama, East Coast USA and East Canada. Mr Isaksen continued, “We offer four sailings per month on fixed dates from the Far East to US/ Canadian Atlantic Ports and in keeping with our philisophy of catering to all transportation modes, the vessels will be able to accommodate unitised general cargo, containers, heavy lifts, rolling stock, refrigerated cargoes and bulk liquids in specially built deeptanks. The new vessels will provide improved loading capacities to all customers including 550/600 TEU’s per sailing and as they are self sustaining, they can call at ports which do not have container cranes. We will, generally speaking, continue to serve ports on a direct basis which we believe is what the customer requires”. The areas covered by BBS are Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Philippines, HongKong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, East and West Canada, US East, West and Gulf Coasts, Panama and Venezuela.

A new container service to Jeddah and Aqaba in the Red Sea started from Tilbury in the Port of London Authority on July 2. The service, which is being run by P & O Strath services, will mean sailings to that part of West Asia from Tilbury every 18 days. Vessels will each be capable of carrying 310 containers. This service is a follow-up of the Arabian Peninsular Container Line Service started recently by P & OStrath-Ellerman jointly with the United Arab Shipping Company. This has sailings every 11 days from Tilbury, and alternatively Liverpool, to Dubai, Muscat, Bahrain and Kuwait.

bodies: In 1842, Smit International started its activities with one paddle tug assisting sailing ships from the North Sea to Rotterdam and back. This modest beginning developed into a worldwide. organisation which is now called the Smit International Group. For years deepsea, coastal and harbour towage, as well as salvage were the mainstay of the company’s activities. With the development of offshore activities, SMIT’s involvements became more numerous and varied with offshore supply services, rig moves, anchor handling, heavy and high lift operations, wreck removal, marine offshore engineering, deepsea diving, underwater survey and maintenance and submersible barge operations. These are just to name some of the Smit International’s worldwide activities.

with the sophisticated equipment and the good spirit of the men executing their task are the key to the success of Smit International. It does not only benefit the clients but is also invaluable to the area they operate in. It goes without saying that, especially in marine salvage, a well executed and swift operation can often mean the prevention of extensive damage to property and to the environment. The combination of the generation old expertise and experience of the Smit International Group together with the local knowledge of their Asian counterpart has become another step towards mutual understanding and success.

Besides the capability and spirit of the men in the company, the equipment is one .very important factor which decides on success or failure. Since its very first days, the Smit International Group has never settled for any inferior quality or inadequate quantity of its equipment. Their tugs, cranes, barges and salvage vessels are all of first class construction and a top standard of maintenance is kept. Since the company operates worldwide, it can afford to carry out constant research for new equipment or methods. The vast experience gained is used to the benefit of each client who requires the service. SS eee Se a ane ens ieee cee Nae a

The Smit International Group realised that their expertise and experience are also required in other parts of the world and therefore a number of operating companies was established all over the world. Naturally, these companies were set up in strategic positions around the globe. For the Far East and South East Asia, the obvious choice was Singapore, the crossroads of the world shipping lanes. Since 1975, Smit International South East Asia has its home in Singapore and during its time of existence has proved its capability, ability for quick response and expertise on numerous occasions. Led by a handful of experienced men from the parent company, a group of some 160 well trained, enthusiastic specialists carry on the tradition of Smit International in Asia. They all have one objective — making their tough and sometime dangerous job a success. All are proud to be members of this outstanding organisation which has integrated them fully into the company’s family, and the company is equally proud to have them under their flag. Good international understanding grooms in an atmosphere of mutual respect and the preparedness to work together on equal basis — all for one and one for all. Working in SMIT is a challenge for the workers and everyone benefits through the efforts of the Group in the true ‘team spirit’. This is a feeling which can only be appreciated when one has to look into the tired but beaming faces of the men who are satisfied to have accomplished a task together and have a right to be proud of it. As expected Smit found this spirit as much in Asia as every where else in the world, the spirit of men who are determined to face the elements and to win.

bodies: CHOOSING THE RIGHT SYSTEM FOR THE BEST PROTECTION For both the shipowner and the shipbuilder the choice of a good paint protection scheme is becoming increasingly important as the prices of steel and labour rise. Ships are becoming more specialised and as a consequence more costly, therefore it is important that shipowners and builders consult their paint supplier before deciding on a system. CONVENTIONAL PAINTS There are many types of paint to choose from; the normal types are Epoxy, Vinyl, Chlorinated Rubber and the so-called conventional. Conventional paints are modernised formulations of the marine paints that have been in existence for many years and invariably consist of primers based on bitumen together with aluminium for underwater surfaces, red lead and zinc chromates for surfaces above water. These primers consist of inorganic pigments which provide good anticorrosive properties to protect your steel. However, a minimum of two coats and preferably three should be applied to obtain the best protection. The primers can be overcoated with antifouling underwater and gloss finishes above water. GRIT BLASTING Before using a Chlorinated Rubber, Epoxy or Vinyl scheme the steel should be grit blasted to Swedish Standard SA2¥%. Immediately after blasting, a coat of Epoxy Blast Primer should be applied. The use of a wash or etch primer based on polyvinylbutyrate is not recommended for the underwater areas and for cargo tanks as they have a tendency to give poor adhesion, once the ship is in service, when used in conjunction with cathodic protection. This will cause an eventual blisting of the subsequent paint system. CHLORINATED RUBBER PAINTS Today there is a great tendency to use Chlorinated Rubber paints, most of which are based on “Alloprene”’, a raw material produced by ICI Mond Division. Chlorinated Rubber (CR) paints incorporate many of the good points of the conventional products, i.e. they include the use of anti-corrosive pigments, but are bonded by a resin containing chlorinated rubber, which is much tougher than the conventional type. CR paints perform extremely well in conjunction with cathodic protection, being able to withstand a greater voltage potential than conventional paints. CHOOSING THE RIGHT SYSTEM FOR THE BEST PROTECTION For both the shipowner and the shipbuilder the choice of a good paint protection scheme is becoming increasingly important as the prices of steel and labour rise. Ships are becoming more specialised and as a consequence more costly, therefore it is important that shipowners and builders consult their paint supplier before deciding on a system. CONVENTIONAL PAINTS There are many types of paint to choose from; the normal types are Epoxy, Vinyl, Chlorinated Rubber and the so-called conventional. Conventional paints are modernised formulations of the marine paints that have been in existence for many years and invariably consist of primers based on bitumen together with aluminium for underwater surfaces, red lead and zinc chromates for surfaces above water. These primers consist of inorganic pigments which provide good anticorrosive properties to protect your steel. However, a minimum of two coats and preferably three should be applied to obtain the best protection. The primers can be overcoated with antifouling underwater and gloss finishes above water. GRIT BLASTING Before using a Chlorinated Rubber, Epoxy or Vinyl scheme the steel should be grit blasted to Swedish Standard SA2¥%. Immediately after blasting, a coat of Epoxy Blast Primer should be applied. The use of a wash or etch primer based on polyvinylbutyrate is not recommended for the underwater areas and for cargo tanks as they have a tendency to give poor adhesion, once the ship is in service, when used in conjunction with cathodic protection. This will cause an eventual blisting of the subsequent paint system. CHLORINATED RUBBER PAINTS Today there is a great tendency to use Chlorinated Rubber paints, most of which are based on “Alloprene”’, a raw material produced by ICI Mond Division. Chlorinated Rubber (CR) paints incorporate many of the good points of the conventional products, i.e. they include the use of anti-corrosive pigments, but are bonded by a resin containing chlorinated rubber, which is much tougher than the conventional type. CR paints perform extremely well in conjunction with cathodic protection, being able to withstand a greater voltage potential than conventional paints. bodies: The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. Swift Electronic Engineers were given the task to install a whole radio room on board the “Golden Season’ belonging to Guan Guan Shipping and the ‘Kota Tanjong” belonging to Pacific International Line. The company has the following subsidiaries, UNI Swift Engineering offering services in motors, generators, winches and pumps, ship’s electrical wiring and marine engine repairs. Lybron (S) Pte Ltd, is the sole agent for Sonneborn Chemstruction Systems of USA, and UCO Swift Engineering Ltd, — “the only local radio company to have an operational office in Bahrain,” the Managing Director said proudly. “The chances of the shipping industry picking up in Singapore are good, but it will take time. Our main market at the moment is Indonesia but later developments can change this situation,” Mr Charlie Hoon concluded.

SELCO SALVAGE LTD. has expanded and diversified its. 1 marine activities from January 1975 to the present date. The increasing size of the fleet has enabled an extensive ocean towage and d salvage coverage of the Indian Ocean to be established, complement- J ing the traditional South China Sea/South East Asian operating area u of the SELCO GROUP. The last twelve months have seen the acquisi- 4 tion of two ocean salvage tugs (of 5500 and 6000 I.H.P. respectively); the laying down and completion of two 1350 I.H.P. sea-going tugs; the launch and completion of two 2750 I.H.P. salvage tugs; and the commissioning of the 2750 I.H.P. twin screw shallow draft specially 1 designed salvage and mooring vessel SALVIKING. The last five s vessels were all built at SELCO (SHIPYARD) PTE. LTD. in ; Singapore. s After an unprecedented series of major tanker salvage operations performed z during 1974, when salvage services were rendered to six heavily damaged or in stranded supertankers, the successful salvage of the 237,500 ton dwt. V.L.C.C. z “SHOWA MARU” in January/February 1975 was a highlight of SELCO’S tanker q salvage operations. With a considerable percentage of the world’s V.L.C.C. and : tanker tonnage since being laid up there has been an inevitable decline in tanker ; casualties requiring salvage assistance. This decline has been offset by much 4 increased commercial towing operations with the enlarged fleet. A down turn in oil exploration and construction in South East Asia has also caused a change in the tug and barge transport operations of the SELCO GROUP. Barges of up G to 10,000 tons previously employed within the South East Asian oil industry are now being utilised for long distance transportation. The 5,000 ton deck 6 cargo “SELCO L-27” with a deck load of 12 barges and other heavy equipment i was towed from Singapore to Iran by the motor salvage tug SALVICEROY. The entire operation — loading, securing, towage preparation, the ocean towage and subsequent discharge at Iran — was performed by SELCO on a package deal basis. Utilising large deck barges as submersible or semi-submersible pontoons operated by the salvage tug crews effects considerable savings for clients. Latest acquisitions and new buildings include 6 tugs and one twin screw motor salvage vessel — the Salviking. SALVIKING was designed by SELCO staff in the light of extensive experience with C.B.M., S.B.M. and other special mooring installations. It has two 80 ton main winches serving the foredeck bow horns, a double drum 25 ton stern winch and a 15 ton swinging derrick. Bow lifts up to 250 tons are possible using specially designed deck tackles which can also be used as ground tackle to exert a horizontal pull exceeding 150 tons. SALVIKING has a long completely clear foredeck enabling chains, hose systems and cables to be worked without difficulty. The vessel is now based in Bahrain to provide its specialised ( services in the Gulf. Salvage/Ocean Rescue The increasing area covered by SELCO is illustrated by the intensive employment of SALVALIANT in July and August 1975. SALVALIANT was assisting “COLOMBO LU” on 25th July from which she was relieved to go to the Pussur River Bar to salvage the motor vessel “OCEAN FRIEND”. The particularly difficult and hazardous work involved commenced on Ist August and “OCEAN FRIEND” was refloated on 6th August. SALVALIANT then went to the South Coast of Ceylon to the disabled coaster “JANI I”’, at that time at the mercy of the South West monsoon. She connected to the “JANI I” on 11th August and towed her to the coast of Ceylon 160 miles away and after leaving her safely anchored, proceeded to the Seychelles where she connected to the “MINGREN SUCCESS” on 20th August and towed the latter to Mauritius. After seven days on station in Mauritius SALVALIANT returned to Singapore to tow a vessel to Taiwan. SALVALIANT’S seven weeks trip involved a total steaming distance of over 8,600 miles and the successful salvaging of several valuable ships and their cargoes. Strandings In addition to the “SHOWA MARU” which has already received much press mention SELCO refloated numerous other stranded vessels, of which one of the most interesting cases was the salvage of the “SHINJITSU MARU” in March 1976. The ““SHINJITSU MARU” grounded at a speed in excess of 15 knots on Pu. Nipa, a coral reef in Indonesian waters close to Singapore. The 7,013 tons gross motor cargo vessel was in ballast, and grounded on the top of high water on the first day of the three-day spring tide period. Her trim was such that she “planed” up the reef coming to rest high and dry forward and heavily aground over 80% of her length. The vessel had very little fuel and no cargo on board so that only heavy ground tackle, speedily deployed, could refloat the vessel during the spring tide period. If the attempt had failed the “SHINJITSU MARU” would have been stranded until the next high spring tide period in April. SELCO despatched the Singapore station salvage vessel SALVIPER which was on site 7 hours after the stranding; and to assist her the heavy salvage and mooring vessel SALVIKING

Whittaker Corporation’s Survival Systems Division, of La Mesa, California, 'U.S.A., says this new vessel, fitted with a fourth-cylinder Perkins diesel, is capable of a getaway speed exceeding six knots. The capsule is equipped with compressed air capable of running the engine for six minutes and providing positive cabin pressure; this system switches automatically to outside air when the compressed air supply is depleted. An air regeneration canister is also provided to revitalise the air by replacing exhaled carbon dioxide with oxygen. Whittaker has fitted the 50-man capsule _—_with throttle/gear shift controls both fore and aft, permitting operation from either station. The operator in the aft station can observe and co-ordinate cable hookup during retrieval. Whittaker’s Survival Systems Division at La Mesa, California, has developed a completed survival and rescue system in tandem with its capsule. Other elements of the system include a holding and launch platform easily installed to the side of a tig; the platform’s electrical system; and a launch/retrieval winch. Fitted with a wide range of safety gear and hung from the side of a rig, the Whittaker capsule can be safely launched into heavy seas from a height of 60 feet in 30 seconds. The craft is quickly retrievable with the system’s electric winch and simple cable hook. Two smaller models with capacities of 14 and 28 men — are also available. The capsule’s dome — brightly painted in international orange — contains four hinged doors, three hatchways, _ ventilating manifolds, sprinkler pipes and manifolds, handrails, and double-paned windows with safety glass inside and wire-reinforced glass _outside. Whittaker has outfitted its new capsule with survival items — from life jackets, fire extinguisher and bailer to signal mirror, food and water, smoke signals and parachute flares with pistol, for those with no choice but to abandon their offshore platform, it is the safest way to go.

A new form of protection is offered to crews on offshore drilling rigs in the event of disaster at sea. Whittaker Corporation of California USA, has introduced a diesel-powered, 50-man survival capsule capable of getaway speeds of more than six knots. Shaped like an elongated flying saucer, the Whittaker capsule is powered by a Perkins 4.15 marine diesel engine, a four-cylinder, in-line unit that develops 62 horsepower. The capsule measures 6 meters long, 3.16 meters high and 4.27 meters wide. Fully loaded with people and provisions, it weighs approximately 7.7 metric tons. Money is important for the private investigator to survive but a good majority of them earn it through honest and dedicated service. It would be interesting to hear comments on “Industrial Security” from readers and the private investigators.

Rapid industrialisation, in any country, leaves in its wake many ill effects. These lead to the necessity for increased surveillance. In Singapore, of late, there has been an increase in the number of companies specialising in industrial security but also in private investigations. Many of these firms have chalked up remarkable successes in not only preventing crimes, as it were, but also bringing to justice culprits after an offence had been committed. A private investigator, who declined to be named, we spoke to said, “Its amazing that a lot of companies in Singapore do not bother to check on the background of applicants for top positions. In my opinion checks should be made before employment and for promotional purposes. Mind you, I am not saying that all applicants etc, are dishonest, but what if you have hired one? Food for thought this. It would appear,that the old adage “prevention is better than cure” is the clue to solving this ever present inconvenience and embarrassment. No reputable company likes its name to be bandied around in the courts of law for want of better care. There are countless crimes being committed by employees in just about every firm. Some of the common ones are kickbacks, pilferage and outright hand-in-gloves at thievery and robbery. All this can be minimised at least, if not, stopped, if only a little more care and attention were paid to security. Not yet rampant but beginning to loom its head in Singapore is industrial espionage which takes the form of counterfeit at the moment. Prone to this are mainly consumer products. But it is not uncommon to find trade marks and patents being infringed. The legal process to disentangle from these is expensive, product-wise damaging, time-consum- “yg and embarrassing to say the least. Admittedly, it is not easy to avoid trademark and patent infringements but expert advice from security and other allied counsultants would reduce the tisk. This again is, perhaps, where private investigators can be of service. Mr W D Anthony, a private investigator and security expert himself said, “A consultant should be a person who can give unbiased, unprejudiced advice entirely to the benefit of the client.” Private investigators charge according to the advice given. However, there are always those who are unscrupulous in every trade.

Sixty New Zealand companies will participate in a New Zealand Industries Trade Exhibition to be held at the Shangri-La Hotel from August 1 to 6 in Singapore. Exhibitors were equally divided between those with established trading links with Singapore and other South East Asian countries and those entering the market for the first time. The exhibits represented four main categories, divided evenly into consumer products, foodstuffs, light engineering items and building materials. The exhibition, the largest national trade show held in the Asean region by New Zealand, will be attended by New Zealand trade commissioners from Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand. A wide range of fire-fighting and industrial safety equipment will be displayed at the New Zealand Industries Exhibition. The exhibitor, M.S. Martin & Co. Ltd., manufactures hose reels and fittings to meet British, Australian and local specifications. The reels are designed to take up to 120 feet of %-inch rubber hose, or 100 feet of 1-inch hose. With an inlet pressure of 30 psi, the latter throws a jet of water 20 feet at a rate of six gallons per minute. The Martin reel is available with a wide range of necessary fittings for various purposes. It is usually supplied without the hose. The company also offers a full range of thermal and smoke detector fire-alarm panels, solid-state security systems and burglar alarms, fire bridage hose and fittings, sprinkler systems and fire extinguishers, industrial hose, and special industrial safety clothing.

annotations.text: Qualified Marine Electronics Technicians Shortage

The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. Swift Electronic Engineers were given the task to install a whole radio room on board the “Golden Season’ belonging to Guan Guan Shipping and the ‘Kota Tanjong” belonging to Pacific International Line. The company has the following subsidiaries, UNI Swift Engineering offering services in motors, generators, winches and pumps, ship’s electrical wiring and marine engine repairs. Lybron (S) Pte Ltd, is the sole agent for Sonneborn Chemstruction Systems of USA, and UCO Swift Engineering Ltd, — “the only local radio company to have an operational office in Bahrain,” the Managing Director said proudly. “The chances of the shipping industry picking up in Singapore are good, but it will take time. Our main market at the moment is Indonesia but later developments can change this situation,” Mr Charlie Hoon concluded.

SELCO SALVAGE LTD. has expanded and diversified its. 1 marine activities from January 1975 to the present date. The increasing size of the fleet has enabled an extensive ocean towage and d salvage coverage of the Indian Ocean to be established, complement- J ing the traditional South China Sea/South East Asian operating area u of the SELCO GROUP. The last twelve months have seen the acquisi- 4 tion of two ocean salvage tugs (of 5500 and 6000 I.H.P. respectively); the laying down and completion of two 1350 I.H.P. sea-going tugs; the launch and completion of two 2750 I.H.P. salvage tugs; and the commissioning of the 2750 I.H.P. twin screw shallow draft specially 1 designed salvage and mooring vessel SALVIKING. The last five s vessels were all built at SELCO (SHIPYARD) PTE. LTD. in ; Singapore. s After an unprecedented series of major tanker salvage operations performed z during 1974, when salvage services were rendered to six heavily damaged or in stranded supertankers, the successful salvage of the 237,500 ton dwt. V.L.C.C. z “SHOWA MARU” in January/February 1975 was a highlight of SELCO’S tanker q salvage operations. With a considerable percentage of the world’s V.L.C.C. and : tanker tonnage since being laid up there has been an inevitable decline in tanker ; casualties requiring salvage assistance. This decline has been offset by much 4 increased commercial towing operations with the enlarged fleet. A down turn in oil exploration and construction in South East Asia has also caused a change in the tug and barge transport operations of the SELCO GROUP. Barges of up G to 10,000 tons previously employed within the South East Asian oil industry are now being utilised for long distance transportation. The 5,000 ton deck 6 cargo “SELCO L-27” with a deck load of 12 barges and other heavy equipment i was towed from Singapore to Iran by the motor salvage tug SALVICEROY. The entire operation — loading, securing, towage preparation, the ocean towage and subsequent discharge at Iran — was performed by SELCO on a package deal basis. Utilising large deck barges as submersible or semi-submersible pontoons operated by the salvage tug crews effects considerable savings for clients. Latest acquisitions and new buildings include 6 tugs and one twin screw motor salvage vessel — the Salviking. SALVIKING was designed by SELCO staff in the light of extensive experience with C.B.M., S.B.M. and other special mooring installations. It has two 80 ton main winches serving the foredeck bow horns, a double drum 25 ton stern winch and a 15 ton swinging derrick. Bow lifts up to 250 tons are possible using specially designed deck tackles which can also be used as ground tackle to exert a horizontal pull exceeding 150 tons. SALVIKING has a long completely clear foredeck enabling chains, hose systems and cables to be worked without difficulty. The vessel is now based in Bahrain to provide its specialised ( services in the Gulf. Salvage/Ocean Rescue The increasing area covered by SELCO is illustrated by the intensive employment of SALVALIANT in July and August 1975. SALVALIANT was assisting “COLOMBO LU” on 25th July from which she was relieved to go to the Pussur River Bar to salvage the motor vessel “OCEAN FRIEND”. The particularly difficult and hazardous work involved commenced on Ist August and “OCEAN FRIEND” was refloated on 6th August. SALVALIANT then went to the South Coast of Ceylon to the disabled coaster “JANI I”’, at that time at the mercy of the South West monsoon. She connected to the “JANI I” on 11th August and towed her to the coast of Ceylon 160 miles away and after leaving her safely anchored, proceeded to the Seychelles where she connected to the “MINGREN SUCCESS” on 20th August and towed the latter to Mauritius. After seven days on station in Mauritius SALVALIANT returned to Singapore to tow a vessel to Taiwan. SALVALIANT’S seven weeks trip involved a total steaming distance of over 8,600 miles and the successful salvaging of several valuable ships and their cargoes. Strandings In addition to the “SHOWA MARU” which has already received much press mention SELCO refloated numerous other stranded vessels, of which one of the most interesting cases was the salvage of the “SHINJITSU MARU” in March 1976. The ““SHINJITSU MARU” grounded at a speed in excess of 15 knots on Pu. Nipa, a coral reef in Indonesian waters close to Singapore. The 7,013 tons gross motor cargo vessel was in ballast, and grounded on the top of high water on the first day of the three-day spring tide period. Her trim was such that she “planed” up the reef coming to rest high and dry forward and heavily aground over 80% of her length. The vessel had very little fuel and no cargo on board so that only heavy ground tackle, speedily deployed, could refloat the vessel during the spring tide period. If the attempt had failed the “SHINJITSU MARU” would have been stranded until the next high spring tide period in April. SELCO despatched the Singapore station salvage vessel SALVIPER which was on site 7 hours after the stranding; and to assist her the heavy salvage and mooring vessel SALVIKING

Fitted with a wide range of safety gear and hung from the side of a rig, the Whittaker capsule can be safely launched into heavy seas from a height of 60 feet in 30 seconds. The craft is quickly retrievable with the system’s electric winch and simple cable hook. Two smaller models with capacities of 14 and 28 men — are also available. The capsule’s dome — brightly painted in international orange — contains four hinged doors, three hatchways, _ ventilating manifolds, sprinkler pipes and manifolds, handrails, and double-paned windows with safety glass inside and wire-reinforced glass _outside. The basic concept of the heat absorber is nothing new. What is new and good is that the Singapore version is manufactured and assembled in Singapore by a Singaporean. This would make it cheaper all round and maintenance only as far as a telephone. The heat absorber, as the name implies, absorbs radiation heat of the sun to heat the water in its maze of copper piping and plates. An insulated storage tank connected to power supply as well, for sunless periods, maintains the temperature of the heated water. The tank can hold up to 40 gallons of heated water which is just about sufficient for four people to have a shower individually or other wise — remember the energy crisis cartoons of not so long ago? Theoretically the idea is simple — have sun will have hot water — but the actual application is nothing short of a jungle of mathematical formulae. Nonetheless, this is a piece of engineering worth-installing not only in homes but in industries requiring constant and cheap supply of hot water. The equipment is assembled at Equatorial Engineering and installed on site. Actual installation takes only a few days. Ask Farid about it. He is a pleasant man to talk to.

Putting solar heat energy to work has become virtually a mania and many an engineer have put forward many ideas, particularly in the field of solar heat energy storage. Oil is, however still available, albeit expensive with its many storms in a teacup. Energy as such has become a burning issue and the average man is made to pay heavily. This has led to the proliferation of ideas on how to cut down costs on at least domestic electricity bills. The brightest and the most workable solution, at least in part, is to install heat absorbers on house roofs. These heat absorbers provide instant hot water (180 _F) without going through electric water heaters. There is hot water in the kitchen and bathroom and elsewhere if you need it and the authorities are happy you are saving energy. Your pocket is that much richer because you are paying less on electricity. And where do you get this heat absorber? In Singapore, made in Singapore, from R Farid who manufactures, installs and maintains it. Mr Farid is an engineer whose stock-in-trade is refrigeration, air-conditioning and allied services in ships. He is the Technical Director of Equatorial Engineering Pte Limited. In his spare time, Mr Farid developed various component parts of the heat absorber, tested it and had one installed in his home seven years ago — it worked and he saved is still saving. Presently, he is installing a unit in a lovely home in one of the more exclusive housing estates. The owner sounded very enthusiatic about it. Who would not with the prospect of saving money.

The watersports specialists are in town at the Marinescene in Orchard Road. You_name it in aquatic sports and they have it. It’s amazing how much equipment they have in stock. Marinescene is a retail outlet for Borneo Marine the parent company. It started out as, literally, a boat shop selling both pleasure and commercial vessels. Eventually it began to market other equipment required in water sports. In pleasure boats and inflatables Marinescene has such delectables as the sleek fibreglass speed boats like the Sting-Ray 15ss, the V-19, Rapier and the Stilleto. For the extra moneyed there are the plush cabin cruisers from Sea Ray and Reinell. For use as a water workhorse there is The Seabarge 17, a utility fibreglass boat without any of the expensive trimmings.

A power boat from Borneo Marine Showing Its paces Avon products in the form of dinghies, sportsboats, scariders, riverboats, liferafts, lifejackets and bouyancy aids can all be purchased from the shop. The company sells not only boats but Johnson outboard motors as well. They have a range from two to two hundred horsepower. Free advice on the type of engine to fit your boat is available. Just having a Johnson outboard is not enough, you need to have accessories like various gauges to power trim and tilt kits too. For the waterskiing enthusiast Marinescene carries a wide range of top quality skis. They have stocks of leading brands like Maherajah, E.P., Cypress Gardesn and Ron Marks. Waterskiing accessories are also available. These accessories are from SkiMaster, Berkeley and Brad. Infact everything that you can possibly want on a waterskiing trip.

bodies: Newly-built pleasure boats are becoming a common sight on the decks of containerships these days, as the box carriers are proving a safer and faster mode of transport for high-value cargoes. bodies: A RELIABLE and economic method of on-stream analysis for increasing the efficiency of mineral processing is offered by the Australian Mineral Development Laboratories (AMDEL). AMDEL is a contract research organisation providing technical development and consulting services to industry and government in the fields of mineral and material sciences. ‘The on-stream analytical system, using radioisotope immersion probes, has application to heavy metal processing for elements above titanium in the Periodic Table, in larger-scale modern plant. It provides a method of-continuous automatic readout of metal values in process slurry streams, enabling the most efficient operation of mineral processing plant. The highly significant break-through in this new method of analysis has been the Australian development of a range of immersible probes, each housing a detector head assembly, a scintillation counter and a radioisotope source . The probes are designed to measure mineral content and slurry density, with an accuracy practical to the application, using both X-ray fluorescence and X-ray gammaray absorption techniques, while actually immersed in the Process streams. _ The probes aré inexpensive, of rugged construction and easy to install and to replace. Components of the on-stream analytical system are designed and manufactured by AMDEL will research and development support from the Australian Atomic Energy Commission. The Australian Mineral Industry Research Association and the Zinc Corporation. Under the terms of a worldwide agreement, AMDEL carries out the necessary feasibility studies, and designs, manufactures and installs the equipment. The system is sufficiently flexible to allow step-bystep growth from a basic analysis arrangement to one involving fully computerised plant control with feedback from a number of points in the process. Because of this flexibility, the cost of the installation can be effectively controlled to suit the size of the plant. The cost of the equipment, although a half to a third that of competitors, is likely to be about $A113,000 fora typical 3-stream installation. The IOSA immersion probe system has now a proved history of operation for more than five years in Australia and abroad, for copper, lead, zinc, nickel and tin. Ships are becoming more specialised and as a consequence more costly, therefore it is important that shipowners and builders consult their paint supplier before deciding on a system. CONVENTIONAL PAINTS There are many types of paint to choose from; the normal types are Epoxy, Vinyl, Chlorinated Rubber and the so-called conventional. Conventional paints are modernised formulations of the marine paints that have been in existence for many years and invariably consist of primers based on bitumen together with aluminium for underwater surfaces, red lead and zinc chromates for surfaces above water. These primers consist of inorganic pigments which provide good anticorrosive properties to protect your steel. However, a minimum of two coats and preferably three should be applied to obtain the best protection. The primers can be overcoated with antifouling underwater and gloss finishes above water. GRIT BLASTING Before using a Chlorinated Rubber, Epoxy or Vinyl scheme the steel should be grit blasted to Swedish Standard SA2¥%. Immediately after blasting, a coat of Epoxy Blast Primer should be applied. The use of a wash or etch primer based on polyvinylbutyrate is not recommended for the underwater areas and for cargo tanks as they have a tendency to give poor adhesion, once the ship is in service, when used in conjunction with cathodic protection. This will cause an eventual blisting of the subsequent paint system. CR paints perform extremely well in conjunction with cathodic protection, being able to withstand a greater voltage potential than conventional paints. bodies: OPTIMUM PROTECTION In order to obtain optimum protection for several years a minimum dry film thickness of 250 microns should be applied. This can be achieved with two coats of high build primer and then a thin decorative coat to suit the owner’s fleet colour. *. When it comes to maintenance CR paints are ideal because they possess outstanding intercoat adhesion, ie. the bond between successive coats of paint: CR paints dry by solvent evaporation and the solvent exerts a powerful blending and bonding action which welds the system together. This is the case even when the old coat has been exposed for years. The superior incercoat adhesion of CR is clearly demonstrated by these photomicrographs. The interfaces between the two coats of Alkyd and Epoxy are clearly defined. This means that adhesion between the coats in these systems is inferior to that of CR where the blurred interface indicates a greater degree of solvent penetration and consequently better intercoat adhesion. SOLVENT POPPING Up to now Epoxy paints have been more popular than CR paints and the Coal Tar Epoxy type is still very popular for underwater use. However they are losing ground to CR in many parts of the world because they are extremely slow drying in cold weather conditions. Even in Singapore, contrary to common belief held by many shipyards, these paints require about 16 hours before being overcoated if “solvent popping” is to be avoided. “Solvent popping” is caused by the use of solvents trying to escape from a tacky film which has been overcoated too soon. The solvent forces an exit through the next layer and leaves a small pin-hole for the sea water to gain access. This starts blistering eventually is the starting point of corrosion and paint failure. ONE-COAT SYSTEMS In order to save a shipyard labour coats, some manufacturers can offer a pure epoxy priming system which will give a dry film thickness of 250 microns in one coat. These one-coat systems are especially useful for VLCC’s and other large vessels, although they are also being used to advantage on smaller vessels when time-saving is essential. ANTIFOULING The choice of antifouling paint for a vessel is extremely important, and should be considered in relation to the drydock interval. There is little point, for instance, in paying for a two-year antifouling if you have to drydock annually to meet the requirements of the ship’s class. For tankers and bulkers which may do alternate voyages in ballast and load positions it is important to have an antifouling that will be re-activated on re-immersion, for example one based on CR or vinyl binders. Conventional antifoulings should normally not be applied more than 24 hours before the vessel is immersed. If they dry we the leaching process is interfered with, consequently they become less effec- ve. OIL RIGS The offshore oil industry demands more sophisticated coatings, particularly ethyl zinc silicates which provide an extremely tough and durable coating when left exposed. If even greater protection is required they can be overcoated with any of the high performance systems mentioned above. Under normal circumstances it is advisable to apply a thin tie coat between the zinc silicate and the thick coating. This type of system is often used in the “splash zone” of rigs where corrosion can be particularly severe. Even in Singapore, contrary to common belief held by many shipyards, these paints require about 16 hours before being overcoated if “solvent popping” is to be avoided. “Solvent popping” is caused by the use of solvents trying to escape from a tacky film which has been overcoated too soon. The solvent forces an exit through the next layer and leaves a small pin-hole for the sea water to gain access. This starts blistering eventually is the starting point of corrosion and paint failure. ONE-COAT SYSTEMS In order to save a shipyard labour coats, some manufacturers can offer a pure epoxy priming system which will give a dry film thickness of 250 microns in one coat. These one-coat systems are especially useful for VLCC’s and other large vessels, although they are also being used to advantage on smaller vessels when time-saving is essential. ANTIFOULING The choice of antifouling paint for a vessel is extremely important, and should be considered in relation to the drydock interval. There is little point, for instance, in paying for a two-year antifouling if you have to drydock annually to meet the requirements of the ship’s class. For tankers and bulkers which may do alternate voyages in ballast and load positions it is important to have an antifouling that will be re-activated on re-immersion, for example one based on CR or vinyl binders. Conventional antifoulings should normally not be applied more than 24 hours before the vessel is immersed. If they dry we the leaching process is interfered with, consequently they become less effec- ve. OIL RIGS The offshore oil industry demands more sophisticated coatings, particularly ethyl zinc silicates which provide an extremely tough and durable coating when left exposed. If even greater protection is required they can be overcoated with any of the high performance systems mentioned above. Under normal circumstances it is advisable to apply a thin tie coat between the zinc silicate and the thick coating. This type of system is often used in the “splash zone” of rigs where corrosion can be particularly severe. This article is by no means intended to be a comprehensive survey of the types of marine paints and painting systems available. bodies: Besides the capability and spirit of the men in the company, the equipment is one .very important factor which decides on success or failure. Since its very first days, the Smit International Group has never settled for any inferior quality or inadequate quantity of its equipment. Their tugs, cranes, barges and salvage vessels are all of first class construction and a top standard of maintenance is kept. Since the company operates worldwide, it can afford to carry out constant research for new equipment or methods. The vast experience gained is used to the benefit of each client who requires the service. SS eee Se a ane ens ieee cee Nae a

with the sophisticated equipment and the good spirit of the men executing their task are the key to the success of Smit International. It does not only benefit the clients but is also invaluable to the area they operate in. It goes without saying that, especially in marine salvage, a well executed and swift operation can often mean the prevention of extensive damage to property and to the environment. The combination of the generation old expertise and experience of the Smit International Group together with the local knowledge of their Asian counterpart has become another step towards mutual understanding and success.

In 1842, Smit International started its activities with one paddle tug assisting sailing ships from the North Sea to Rotterdam and back. This modest beginning developed into a worldwide. organisation which is now called the Smit International Group. For years deepsea, coastal and harbour towage, as well as salvage were the mainstay of the company’s activities. With the development of offshore activities, SMIT’s involvements became more numerous and varied with offshore supply services, rig moves, anchor handling, heavy and high lift operations, wreck removal, marine offshore engineering, deepsea diving, underwater survey and maintenance and submersible barge operations. These are just to name some of the Smit International’s worldwide activities.

The Smit International Group realised that their expertise and experience are also required in other parts of the world and therefore a number of operating companies was established all over the world. Naturally, these companies were set up in strategic positions around the globe. For the Far East and South East Asia, the obvious choice was Singapore, the crossroads of the world shipping lanes. Since 1975, Smit International South East Asia has its home in Singapore and during its time of existence has proved its capability, ability for quick response and expertise on numerous occasions. Led by a handful of experienced men from the parent company, a group of some 160 well trained, enthusiastic specialists carry on the tradition of Smit International in Asia. They all have one objective — making their tough and sometime dangerous job a success. All are proud to be members of this outstanding organisation which has integrated them fully into the company’s family, and the company is equally proud to have them under their flag. Good international understanding grooms in an atmosphere of mutual respect and the preparedness to work together on equal basis — all for one and one for all. Working in SMIT is a challenge for the workers and everyone benefits through the efforts of the Group in the true ‘team spirit’. This is a feeling which can only be appreciated when one has to look into the tired but beaming faces of the men who are satisfied to have accomplished a task together and have a right to be proud of it. As expected Smit found this spirit as much in Asia as every where else in the world, the spirit of men who are determined to face the elements and to win.

bodies: Since sand was prohibited as a blasting abrasive in November, 1974 on account of the health hazards it causes, particularly the risk of silicosis, copper slag has emerged as the most suitable alternative for the shiprepairing industry. In shiprepairing, where recovery of spent abrasives is difficult because blasting is done in the open, copper slag is eminently suited owing to its low cost. However, in shipbuilding and the construction of oil rigs and other fabrications, where steel plates may be shot-blasted and coated before they are used, steel abrasives are proving increasingly popular. Certain shipyards have already equipped themselves with automatic blasting machines and chambers incorporating abrasive recovery systems, thereby paving the way for the use of steel abrasives which in spite of their higher costs, prove more economical in the longer term because they can be re-used many times. In fact, numerous companies have also been set up to do shot-blasting for others who do not find it economically worthwhile to have their own automatic blasting machines or blasting chambers. Apart from the numerous marine contractors who contract for the cleaning and painting of ships in various shipyards, there are also contractors specialising in industrial blasting work such as those connected with factory structures, installations and pipelines. In the shiprepairing industry, there is an increasing tendency for tankers to call at Singapore for tank internal blasting, an operation which requires not only highly specialised equipment but also abrasives which are sieved according to rather stringent specifications. Pan Abrasives (Private) Limited, which has just moved to its new 3¥-acre site in Jurong, is equipped to supply the needs of shipyards and marine contractors in all forms of blasting abrasives. With a factory capable of producing 12,000 tons of copper slag per month when it is in full production, and with the modern machinery which it has recently installed, it is setting new standards in this important supporting industry. Besides copper slag, they keep a good groundstock of chilled iron abrasive, steel shot and grit, glass beads, aluminium oxide, silicone carbide and a wide range of media and compound. With four large pneumatic tankers, it is equipped to deliver its abrasives in bulk, expeditiously and efficiently, to its customers, factors which are all important to marine contractors and shipyards who frequently work to very tight time schedules. It also has a team of technical personnel trained to provide technical assistance and advice in the use of its products.

bodies: Edgars has been successful in supplying a highly sophisticated range of materials handling system (MHS) providing the Singapore International Airport’s Cargo Terminal the capacity to handle efficiently an anticipated 160,000 tonnes of cargo yearly. A total of four organisations were involved in the development of the system. The organisations were — Singapore Airport Terminal F Services, the American consultancy firm of Breier Neidle Patrone Associates Inc, the contractor for the system — Transact Overseas ¥ Inc, and, of course, Hargill Singapore Pte Limited, Edgar Division. I. Edgar was the main sub-contractor for the local fabrication, erection and commissioning of the system in close collaboration with  ~- Transact Overseas Incorporated’s resident engineer. MHS is semi-mechanised with its most distinctive feature being _ the two Transact-made low-profile transfer vehicles forming the heart of the system. Additional components are the conveyors, forklift trucks, electronic and mechanical weighing scales, docklevellers, scossor lifts, racking and storage boxes. ' In association with Transact Overseas Inc., Edgar met the stringent _ requirement of the job. Edgars’ long standing experience in the field * of material handling came to the fore when the project was complet- P ed in May 1977. The Edgar division of Hargill Singapore Pte. Limited is actually involved in the supply of material handling equipment to the Port of Singapore Authority, the Singapore Airport Terminal Services and other major sea and air ports in the region. Their involvement includes supply, maintenance and installation where necessary. As regards airport equipment they are the sole agent for all the British Airport Equipment (BAE), which is a consortium of Albar Engineering Limited, Norwich Coachworks Limited, Hydro-Hygiene Services Limited, Power Lifts Limited and A.C.S. Engineering Sales Limited, all of United Kingdom. BAE manufacturers a very comprehensive range of airport equipment. Typical are airtugs, towing tractors, hydraulic lifting platforms, container pallet dollies, mobile aircraft maintenance platforms, toilet and water servicing units, aircraft exterior cleaning units, commissary trucks, mobile baggage loaders and Passenger stairs. All this equipment is available from Edgar. Over the past few years, Edgar supplied over 80 units of Reliance Mercury tractors to Singapore and Malaysian seaports and airports. As agents of Rubery-Owen Karritainers Limited UK, Edgar supplied a total 20 straddle carriers and one travel-lift to Singapore and Malaysia Ports. The straddle carriers, equipped with telescopic spreader easily handles 20ft to 40ft containers stacking them 3-high. The company also acts as agent for marketing and maintaining the complete range of Mitsubishi forklift trucks. The lifting capacity of these forklifts is from 1350 kg (2700 Ibs) to 15,000 kg (33,000 Ibs.) These forklifts are generally well received with a record of high performance and reliability. The biggest users of this equipment are ports followed by various industries and warehousing companies. The Mitsubishi forklifts are either diesel or LPG driven. The company also deals in NYK electric forklift trucks. Available in the range are reach trucks and counter balanced trucks with capacities ranging from 500 kg to 3000 kg. Maintenance on these trucks is made easy by unitizing easily replaceable components. Some models have built-in automatic chargers. The third brand of forklifts that Edgars market is the “Rolls Royce” of this workhorse clan. This is the climax — Conveyancer forklift trucks made in England. Most popular of the diesel range are — the TC 6 lifting 2750 kg (6000 Ib). the TC 7 lifting 3200 kg (7000 Ib) and the TC 8 lifting 3660 kg (8000 Ib). These forklifts are performed by companies which are familiar with their reliability

Melbourne, AUSTRALIA — Solar energy is to be used to bring both telephone and television to a remote area of the vast Australia inland. Electricity generated by solar energy will power 13 repeater stations which will be hooked into Australia’s extensive microwave trunk system carrying telephone, television, and cable communications. ‘ The power " engineers from Telecom Australia, the Government statutory organisation which runs Australia’s telephone and communication system, have spent three years researching and developing the novel concept of solar energy powering a major multipurpose telecommunications system.

Hydro Products’ SeaTrak Current Meter System offers a complete service for obtaining basic oceanographic data. It is a precision tool designed for a variety of applications including sea floor mounting, taut line mooring and making current profiles from a ship. The standard Sea Trak measures and records current speed, direction, elapsed time and a user selected identification digit on easy to handle cassettes. When coupled with the Sea Trak Data Processor, it reduces recorded information on site into almost any output recording device or directly into a computer for high speed data analysis. The Data Processor also performs a complete selftest and self-check with its own built-in diagnostic tester. The Exclusive Far East Agent for SEATRAK is James Gauntt Pte. Ltd.

bodies: The Managing Director of Swift Electronic Engineers, Mr Charlie Hoon, feels that there is an overall shortage of experienced technicians in the marine electronics field. He said, “There is no shortage of lettered technicians, by this I mean technicians who have completed technical school or even college courses. But what the marine electronics industry needs, and urgently, is technicians who have practical experience and are willing to go on acquiring skills.”’ Mr Hoon feels that while it is good to have theoretical knowledge it should not be forgotten that the technician is required at a work site on a piece of equipment and not with a pen and paper in his hands. “College graduates must think of themselves as technicians first and administrators second. It is only after knowing what is happening at the grease-pot level that an academically qualified technician can become an administrator fit to give instructions,” the Managing Director continued. Work in any kind of engineering establishment, particularly in the marine field, has rather odd working hours, but it is rather unfortunate that a lot of technical employees in these organisations prefer to keep to fixed working hours. Swift Electronic Engineers, which employs a large number of specialised marine electronics technicians is perhaps the only company in Singapore which can repair gyro-compasses. The company has had to send several of its staff to Japan and the United States of America for basic and advanced training in the maintenance and repair of various brands in radar, single-sideband radio-telephone, VHF, transmitters and receivers, and echo sounders. They carry a very wide range of spare parts and offer twenty-four hour service. “There have been occasions when we have been so short of technical staff that I’ve had to attend to repair and installation jobs myself,” said Mr Hoon who holds A.LP.R.E. and 2nd class P.M.G. Swift Electronic Engineers were given the task to install a whole radio room on board the “Golden Season’ belonging to Guan Guan Shipping and the ‘Kota Tanjong” belonging to Pacific International Line. The company has the following subsidiaries, UNI Swift Engineering offering services in motors, generators, winches and pumps, ship’s electrical wiring and marine engine repairs. Lybron (S) Pte Ltd, is the sole agent for Sonneborn Chemstruction Systems of USA, and UCO Swift Engineering Ltd, — “the only local radio company to have an operational office in Bahrain,” the Managing Director said proudly. “The chances of the shipping industry picking up in Singapore are good, but it will take time. Our main market at the moment is Indonesia but later developments can change this situation,” Mr Charlie Hoon concluded.

Redifon also manufacture high quality marine V.H.F. including the Sealand 66 with touch keyboard channel selection and facilities for up to five remote control positions. For smaller vessels the Sealand 30, with up to thirty channels is highly successful in many markets. Redifon also supplies Omega and Satellite Navigators and was one of the first companies to manufacture shipboard receivers for both world wide navigation systems. Also available from Kelvin Hughes in South East Asia, is the $.G. Brown range of gyro compasses and autopilots. The Mk. 10 gyro is fitted in many hundreds of ships, including naval vessels of many countries. The heart of this compass is the well proven Arma Brown sensitive element which has a Mean Time Between Failure of 50,000 hours, which gives the Mk. 10 its well deserved reputation for reliability. Hydrographic survey is expected to play an increasing part in the expansion of Kelvin Hughes in South East Asia. Kelvin Hughes Survey is one of the oldest commercial hydrographic organisations in the world. Just over two years ago a decision was taken to set up a branch of Kelvin Hughes Survey in Singapore in order to be able to offer services to its wide range of clients from a base in the region. Survey can now offer its complete capability including surveys for port development and construction, power stations, environmental studies, pipeline and cable routes, pipe-laying, rig and structure positioning and other inshore or offshore civil engineering projects. The association with Compagnie Generale de Geophysique in Anglo-French Offshore Surveys Ltd., has enabled Survey to extend its capability to include position fixing systems, shallow seismic geo physical investigations, oceanographic and meteorological services. The overall market for marine electronics equipment is expected to remain difficult for at least another two years. World trade is increasing relatively slowly and the glut of large tankers will continue to depress shipping markets for some time. In these conditions shipowners will rightly be extremely cost conscious and any products on services which are to succeed in these conditions must offer genuine economic advantages, increased safety, or both. The market for naval equipment is expected to be a growth area in the immediate future. Navies are increasingly turning to smaller high technology warships and Singapore is well placed to obtain a significant share of this market This will in turn effect suppliers, such as Kelvin Hughes, who have traditionally supplied a large proportion of their output to the world’s navies. Current production includes naval navigational radar and sonar systems, featuring the latest technology and designed specifically for naval requirements. A full service capability on all types of equipment is a necessity recognised by firms engaged in the marine electronics industry and the upgrading of the skills of local staff is regarded as sensible for business reasons as well as being socially desirable. Kelvin Hughes frequently sends technicians to Europe to be: brought up to date on the latest equipment and techniques. To sum up, the marine electronics business is a very testing market but backed up with good products and services, tailored to the customers requirements, Kelvin Hughes feels confident in its future in Singapore. An order book running well ahead of 1976 levels gives backing to this view. scfihpickt ieee aaah ee

New Port Facility Nears Completion

At the East Lagoon on the northern side of the PSA container terminal , two new container berths are now under construction. These berths will cater increased container traffic expected in the next few years. The first berth will provide a special shore based ramp designed to service the three new vessels of the ANRO Consortium which comprises the Australian National Line, Neptune Orient Lines of Singapore, Australia Straits Container Line and Nedllyod Lines. Completion of the berth is expected by the end of September 1977.

The two berths totalling about S$66 million will be 640 metres in length with two main access bridges linking them to a 19.5 hectare marshalling yard and 10.5 heotares of back up land. The schedule was 18 months for completion of the first berth and 26 months for the complete project. To date the schedule has been maintained. Although the extra capacity provided by the 2 berths will help equip the terminal to cater for the estimated growth in container traffic between now and 1980, the project has been designed to be as flexible as possible. Four 35 tonne portainer cranes purchased at a cost of about $$2.56 million each, plus several transtainer cranes will service the berths. This equipment combined with the modern gear and design of the vessels will help cater for the growth in cargo traffic by improving turn-around times and collection and delivery of cargo. The two new berths will be equipped and fully operational by 1979 just about the same time the existing facilities will have reached their optimum capacity. The construction of the two new berths coincides with the commencement of work on a $$50 million inland container depot at Bukit Timah, about 25 kilometres from the terminal. Its function will be a container storage area and a break bulk consolidation depot.
